title: Search commit messages, and make them machine-readable
summary: Find every commit mentioning a ticket, then learn the trailer convention that turns commit messages into structured data your release tooling can read.
mental_model: A commit message is a subject line, a blank line, a body, and then trailers — `Key: value` lines at the end. Git treats trailers as a real format, so `Fixes:` and `Co-authored-by:` are parseable rather than just conventional.

setup.run: git commit -q -m "Add pump control" -m "Drives the circulation pump from the schedule table." -m "Refs: ABH-101"

git commit -q -a -m "Fix pump stall at low RPM" -m "The controller stalled below 900 RPM on cold starts." -m "Fixes: ABH-204
Reviewed-by: Priya <priya@shakha.local>"

steps.title: Search the message text
steps.why: `--grep` matches the whole message, subject and body. This is how you find 'that commit about the pump stall' when you cannot remember its sha.
steps.expect: One match for stall, two for pump.

steps.title: Find everything for a ticket
steps.why: Ticket ids in messages become searchable forever. This one command replaces trawling a project-management tool for 'what shipped for ABH-204'.

verify.label: the ticket's commit is findable by id

steps.title: Combine and invert filters
steps.why: Multiple `--grep` options are OR by default; `--all-match` makes them AND. `--invert-grep` finds everything that does NOT match — useful for spotting commits with no ticket reference at all.
steps.expect: The invert search shows the two commits with no ticket id — the ones your process missed.

steps.title: Read the trailers as data
steps.why: `%(trailers)` in a format string extracts the structured lines. `:key=Fixes` pulls out one specific trailer — which is exactly how a changelog generator finds what a release fixed.
steps.expect: Ticket ids and reviewers extracted cleanly, with blanks where there are none.

steps.title: Add a trailer to a new commit properly
steps.why: `--trailer` appends a correctly formatted trailer rather than you hand-typing it into the body. Git handles the blank-line rules, which are the part people get wrong.

actions.run: git commit -q -m "Alert on pH drift" --trailer "Fixes: ABH-301" --trailer "Co-authored-by: Priya <priya@shakha.local>"

verify.label: the new commit carries a parseable Fixes trailer

steps.title: Generate the release notes
steps.why: Filter to commits with a Fixes trailer, print subject and ticket. This is a complete changelog pipeline in one command, with no dependencies and no extra tooling.
steps.expect: A bulleted list with ticket ids — paste-ready.

steps.title: Check a message before committing it
steps.why: `interpret-trailers --parse` reads any message and prints only its trailers. This is what a commit-msg hook uses to enforce 'every commit must reference a ticket'.
steps.expect: Just the Key: value lines, ready for a script to validate.

verify.label: your commit has a machine-readable Fixes trailer
…and credits the co-author in the standard format
four commits reference a ticket and are findable by id

pitfalls: A trailer must be in the last paragraph of the message, with no blank line inside the block. One stray blank line and git stops parsing them.
`--grep` is a regex by default. Search for `ABH-204` and the hyphen is literal, but `.` and `*` are not — use `--fixed-strings` when in doubt.
`Co-authored-by:` is a GitHub convention built on git's trailer format. Git parses it; the attribution on the website is GitHub's own layer.
Squashing commits concatenates their messages, which usually breaks the trailer block. Re-add trailers after a squash.
cheatsheet: read trailers out of any message
